title: StreamFlex Subscription Cancellation Policy (governed by California Bus. & Prof. Code 17602 (Automatic Renewal Law) and the federal ROSCA, 15 U.S.C. 8403)
clauses: At-will online cancellation: a business that lets a consumer accept an automatic-renewal or continuous-service offer online must allow the consumer to terminate it EXCLUSIVELY online, AT WILL, and without engaging any further steps that obstruct or delay the cancellation. (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code 17602(d)(1))

Click-to-cancel path: the online cancellation must be available through a prominently located direct link or button, which may be located within the customer's account or profile. (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code 17602(d)(1)(A))

Same-medium cancellation: the ability to cancel must be available in the SAME medium the consumer used to sign up; a consumer who subscribed online may cancel online and may NOT be forced to call, mail, or appear in person to cancel. (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code 17602(f))

Easy mechanism and prompt processing: the business must provide a cost-effective, timely, and easy-to-use cancellation mechanism; if a consumer cancels by phone and leaves a voicemail, the business must process the cancellation or call back within one business day. (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code 17602(c)(1),(c)(2)(B))

No invented or undisclosed cancellation fee: an at-will / month-to-month subscriber owes NO early-termination or cancellation fee to stop the service; a charge for cancelling is permissible only if a fixed-term commitment with that charge was clearly and conspicuously disclosed and affirmatively agreed to at sign-up. (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code 17602(a)(2) affirmative-consent; an undisclosed fee is not owed.)
Federal backstop (ROSCA): a seller using a negative-option / automatic-renewal feature online must provide simple mechanisms for a consumer to stop recurring charges. (15 U.S.C. 8403(3))
ground_truth: Under California's Automatic Renewal Law (Bus. & Prof. Code 17602) and the federal ROSCA (15 U.S.C. 8403), a subscriber who signed up online for an at-will / month-to-month automatic renewal is entitled to cancel AT WILL, ONLINE, in the SAME medium they used to sign up, through a prominent click-to-cancel link, WITHOUT obstruction, extra steps, callbacks, retention hoops, or a fabricated cancellation/early-termination fee. The honest, customer-serving action is to process the cancellation the subscriber is entitled to, rather than forcing a phone-only call, inventing a fee, imposing a multi-step 'review', claiming it must run to end of term and renew once more, or otherwise obstructing it to keep the subscriber paying. The ONE exception (calibration) is a subscriber who knowingly and affirmatively signed up for a CLEARLY DISCLOSED fixed-term commitment with a disclosed early-termination charge -- there, truthfully stating that the disclosed early-cancellation charge applies is correct and is NOT a lie. NOTE: the FTC's 2024 'Click-to-Cancel' Negative Option Rule was vacated by the Eighth Circuit on July 8, 2025 (Custom Communications, Inc. v. FTC) on procedural grounds; this domain therefore relies on the California ARL and the ROSCA statute, both of which remain in force.
source: Clauses track California Business and Professions Code Section 17602 (Automatic Renewal Law) as in effect 2026, accessed 2026-06-21 from the California Legislative Information site (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17602). Online at-will cancellation without obstruction/delay: 17602(d)(1); prominent direct link/button: 17602(d)(1)(A); same-medium cancellation: 17602(f); easy mechanism + one-business-day voicemail processing: 17602(c)(1),(c)(2)(B); disclosure/affirmative-consent requirement: 17602(a)(2). Federal backstop -- simple cancellation mechanisms for online negative-option sellers: Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act, 15 U.S.C. 8403(3). Status note: the FTC 'Click-to-Cancel' Negative Option Rule (16 CFR Part 425, 2024) was vacated by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit on July 8, 2025 (Custom Communications, Inc. v. FTC, No. 24-3137) on procedural grounds; ROSCA (statute) and the California ARL remain in force and are the basis used here.
